title: Scotch Broth
subtitle: Slow-cooked lamb soup with root vegetables and bulgur wheat
excerpt: Scotch broth is a thick, warming soup built on a long-simmered lamb stock with root vegetables and whole grain. Pearl barley is the traditional grain; bulgur wheat gives a similar hearty texture and cooks in a fraction of the time. This is a soup that improves the next day once it has had a chance to sit and deepen.
sourceNotes: Scotch broth has been eaten in Scotland for centuries as a way to extract flavour from tougher cuts of mutton or lamb. Early versions were simply meat simmered in water with whatever root vegetables were available; the addition of grain came later as a way to add body and extend the dish.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. The bulgur wheat absorbs liquid as it sits; add a splash of hot water when reheating.

content.text: Brown the lamb properly before adding the liquid. The colour and flavour from browning is what gives the broth its depth. Do not rush this step.

items.prepNote: used in place of traditional pearl barley

content.text: Place the diced lamb in the stockpot over high heat with a drizzle of oil. Brown in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per batch until coloured on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Add the onion, carrot, celery, leek, and parsnip to the same pot. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes, scraping up any browned bits from the base.
Return the lamb to the pot and pour over the chicken stock. Add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Skim off any foam that rises to the surface.

Cover and simmer for 1 hour until the lamb is tender. Add the bulgur wheat, stir well, and continue simmering uncovered for a further 15 minutes until the bulgur is cooked and the broth has thickened.
Remove the bay leaves. Taste and adjust seasoning generously with salt and black pepper. Ladle into deep bowls and scatter the chopped parsley over the top.

items.symptom: The lamb is still chewy after an hour
items.cause: Lamb shoulder has a lot of connective tissue that needs sustained heat to break down
items.fix: Continue simmering, covered, in 15-minute increments until the meat is tender. A slow cooker on low for 6 hours also works well.

items.cause: The lid was on throughout, preventing reduction, or the bulgur was not added
items.fix: Remove the lid and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes. The bulgur will continue to absorb liquid and thicken the soup as it sits.
